headline: A College Tried to Remove Security Cameras, But the Company Wouldn't Let Them

levels.label: Grade 3-4
levels.summary: A college in Illinois called Elgin Community College put up six safety cameras made by a company named Flock. The cameras were supposed to help keep students safe. But later, the school found out that Flock might be sharing camera information with other groups, and that the cameras were not being kept safe from people who shouldn't see them. The school asked Flock to take the cameras down. Flock said no, because the school still had a contract, which is like a signed promise to use their cameras for a certain amount of time. The school even offered to pay for the rest of the time left on the contract, but Flock still would not remove them. So workers at the school covered the cameras with black trash bags and zip ties so they couldn't record anything. But mystery workers kept sneaking back and taking the bags off! This went back and forth for months. Finally, in April, the contract ended, and Flock took the cameras away. This story shows how tricky it can be when a company controls something a school wants to stop using.

levels.label: Grade 5-6
levels.summary: Elgin Community College in Illinois installed six security cameras from a company called Flock in 2025 to help keep students safe. But soon, the school started worrying about how the cameras were being used. They learned that Flock might be sharing camera footage with federal border police, that the video feeds weren't protected very well, and that both police and Flock's own workers may have misused the camera data. Because of these worries, the school asked Flock to remove the cameras. Flock said no, because the school was still under contract, a legal agreement that said the cameras would stay for a set amount of time. The school even offered to pay the rest of the contract's cost just to get the cameras removed early, but Flock didn't respond. So the school's staff got creative: they covered the cameras with black trash bags and tied them shut with zip ties so the cameras couldn't record. But someone in an unmarked car, likely working for Flock, kept sneaking onto campus and taking the covers off. This cycle of covering and uncovering repeated for months until the contract finally ended in April, and Flock removed the cameras for good. This story raises real questions about who controls surveillance technology on school campuses, and what happens when a company refuses to listen to the people it's supposed to serve.

levels.label: Grade 7-8
levels.summary: In 2025, Elgin Community College in Illinois had six security cameras installed by a company called Flock. The cameras were meant to improve safety on campus. But by the fall, school leaders grew concerned about how the cameras were actually being used. They worried that Flock might be sharing footage with federal immigration and border enforcement agencies, that the video feeds weren't properly protected from hackers or unauthorized viewers, and that both police and Flock employees might be misusing access to the footage. Because of these concerns, the college asked Flock to take the cameras down. Flock refused, arguing it hadn't broken any part of its contract, the legal agreement outlining the terms of the camera installation. Months later, the school tried again, this time offering to pay for the remaining five months left on the contract just to end the arrangement early. Flock didn't even respond. That's when the situation got strange. School staff began covering the cameras with black trash bags secured by zip ties to physically block them from recording. However, people in an unmarked vehicle, who the school's president believed worked for Flock, kept returning to campus and removing the coverings. This back-and-forth, covering the cameras and having them uncovered, continued for several months. It wasn't until April 2026, when the original contract finally expired, that Flock removed the cameras entirely. This story highlights a growing concern across the country: once a school, city, or organization installs surveillance technology from a private company, it may be very difficult to remove it, even if serious privacy or safety concerns arise. It raises important questions about who truly controls these systems, and what rights customers have when they want to stop using a technology they've grown uncomfortable with.

levels.label: Grade 9-10
levels.summary: In April 2025, Elgin Community College in Illinois installed six security cameras made by a company called Flock Safety, intending to boost safety and security for students. By September, however, administrators became alarmed. They learned that Flock might be sharing surveillance data with Customs and Border Patrol, a federal agency, that the camera feeds weren't adequately secured from outside access, and that both law enforcement officials and Flock's own employees may have been misusing their access to footage. These concerns led the college to formally request that Flock remove the cameras in October 2025. According to the college's president, Peggy Heinrich, Flock refused, stating that it hadn't violated any terms of its contract, the legal agreement specifying how long and under what conditions the cameras would remain installed. Two months later, in December, the school tried a different approach: it offered to pay the cost of the contract's remaining five months just to get the cameras taken down sooner. This offer was met with total silence from Flock. Frustrated by the lack of response, college staff took matters into their own hands. They covered the cameras with black trash bags, securing them with zip ties, to physically prevent the devices from recording anything. But according to Heinrich, people driving an unmarked vehicle, who she believed worked for Flock, kept returning to campus to remove the coverings, restoring the cameras' ability to record. This odd standoff repeated multiple times over several months: the school would cover the cameras, and the mystery workers would uncover them again. The situation wasn't resolved until April 2026, when the original contract finally expired and Flock removed the cameras from campus altogether. This incident sheds light on a broader, increasingly relevant issue: as schools, cities, and businesses adopt surveillance technology from private companies, they may find themselves with far less control than expected. Even when legitimate privacy or ethical concerns arise, contracts can leave customers stuck with technology they no longer want, unable to simply walk away until an agreement's terms are fully satisfied. It also raises uncomfortable questions about consent, oversight, and what recourse an institution has when a technology vendor refuses to cooperate, even informally circumventing physical barriers put up by the customer itself.

levels.label: Grade 11+
levels.summary: In April 2025, Elgin Community College in Illinois installed six surveillance cameras made by Flock Safety, a company that provides automated camera systems often marketed to schools, neighborhoods, and police departments as tools to enhance public safety. The stated purpose was to improve security for students and staff on campus. However, by September 2025, college administrators grew increasingly uneasy. They discovered that Flock may have been sharing captured data with Customs and Border Patrol, a federal immigration enforcement agency, raising concerns about how student and community data might be used beyond its original safety purpose. Additionally, officials found that the camera feeds were not adequately secured against unauthorized access, and that both law enforcement personnel and Flock's own employees may have inappropriately accessed or misused the footage. In response, the college formally requested in October 2025 that Flock remove the cameras from its property. According to college President Peggy Heinrich, Flock declined, asserting that it had not breached any terms of its contract, the binding legal agreement establishing the conditions and duration of the camera installation. The college persisted, and in December 2025 offered to pay the costs for the remaining five months left on the contract, essentially proposing to buy their way out of the agreement early in exchange for the cameras' immediate removal. Flock did not respond to this offer at all. Faced with an unresponsive vendor and an active surveillance system they no longer trusted, the college's staff resorted to a direct, physical solution: covering the cameras with black plastic trash bags and securing them with zip ties to block the lenses from recording. Remarkably, according to reporting from the Chicago Sun-Times, individuals in an unmarked vehicle, who Heinrich believed were affiliated with Flock, repeatedly returned to campus to remove these coverings, apparently to maintain the cameras' functionality despite the college's clear wishes. This resulted in a prolonged standoff in which school staff would re-cover the cameras, only to have them uncovered again during what Flock may have characterized as routine service visits. The dispute wasn't resolved through any formal agreement or negotiation, but simply through the natural expiration of the original contract in April 2026, at which point Flock finally removed the cameras entirely. This episode illustrates a significant and growing tension in the deployment of surveillance technology by private companies within public institutions. It demonstrates how contractual relationships can leave customers, even entities like schools with legitimate oversight responsibilities, with surprisingly limited practical control over technology once it's installed. The incident also raises serious questions about corporate accountability, data privacy, and the ethical obligations companies have when their customers express clear, repeated objections to how a product or service is being used. For communities considering similar surveillance partnerships, this case serves as a cautionary example of how difficult it can be to reverse course once such systems are in place.

questions: If you found out cameras at your school might be sharing information with outside groups without clear permission, how would you want your school to respond?
Why do you think it might be hard for a school or city to remove technology from a company once it's already installed, even if they have real safety or privacy concerns?
What rules or protections do you think should exist to make sure companies listen to schools, communities, or customers who want to stop using their technology?
